metadata.description: Parallel rediscovery of the same multilayer back-propagation algorithm. Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams (1986) derive BP via direct chain-rule bookkeeping over a layered sigmoidal network with squared-error loss; Le Cun (1988) re-derives the identical algorithm as the stationarity conditions of a Lagrange function whose Lagrange multipliers are the adjoint/costate variables. The forward dynamics, backward recursion, output-layer boundary condition, and gradient-descent weight update appear in both papers; Le Cun additionally embeds the recurrent (Pineda-Almeida) variant in the same Lagrangian framework, while Rumelhart et al. handle recurrence by unrolling and extend the algorithm with momentum and worked examples (symmetry, family-tree, BPTT).

matches.explanation: Both define the same object: a layered feed-forward network with per-layer weight matrices and componentwise nonlinearity. Le Cun's $A_p(k) = W(k) X_p(k-1)$ is the matrix form of Rumelhart's $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$ (EP207.1). Rumelhart's bias-as-weight convention (DP207.3) is implicit in Le Cun's $W(k)$ matrices. Both PDFs reduce LaTeX fidelity, so the match is on names/types/roles, not exact symbols.

The notion of a 'hidden unit' as the units whose representations must be discovered is a central conceptual framing in Rumelhart et al. Le Cun's framework treats all internal layers uniformly via the constraint structure and never isolates 'hidden units' as a distinguished concept; the representation-learning narrative is absent from his formal treatment.

Le Cun's defining novelty is the Lagrange function $L(W,X,B) = C(X(N)) + \sum_k B(k)^T (X(k) - F[W(k) X(k-1)])$ that enforces the forward equations as constraints via Lagrange multipliers $B(k)$. Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams have no analogous object; they apply the chain rule directly to the error $E$ without reformulating it as a constrained optimization problem.

The costate / adjoint variable $Y_p(k) = \nabla F_k(A_p(k)) B_p(k)$ is Le Cun's bridge between the Lagrange multipliers and the standard back-propagated 'delta' quantities. Rumelhart et al. compute the analogous quantity $\partial E / \partial x_j$ directly in EP207.5 but do not introduce a named costate variable, so there is no node-level counterpart even though the underlying numerical quantity coincides.

The Hamiltonian $H_p(k) = B_p(k)^T F[W(k) X_p(k-1)]$ and its conjugate-variable interpretation (RP206.2) have no counterpart in Rumelhart et al., who never invoke optimal-control or Hamiltonian formalism.

Both papers handle weight sharing / equality constraints among weights, but with very different scope. Le Cun treats it generally by reparameterizing $W = W(U,k)$ and deriving the chain-rule update $u_q \leftarrow u_q + \lambda \sum y_i x_j \partial w_{ij}/\partial u_q$. Rumelhart et al. show one concrete instance: averaging $\partial E/\partial w$ over time-replicated copies in an unrolled recurrent net. Same underlying mechanism (sum gradients of tied weights) applied to different cases.

The recurrent-network Hamiltonian $H = C(X) + B^T[X - F(WX)]$ used by Le Cun to re-derive Pineda-Almeida fixed-point gradients has no analogue in Rumelhart et al., who handle recurrence only via unrolling-in-time (ExP207.3).

Forward dynamics. Le Cun's $X_p(k) = F_k[W(k) X_p(k-1)]$ is the matrix-form composition of Rumelhart's $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$ followed by $y_j = 1/(1+e^{-x_j})$. Same equation, different granularity (vector vs scalar).

Output-layer boundary condition. Le Cun's $B_p(N) = 2(D_p - X_p(N))$ matches Rumelhart's $\partial E/\partial y_j = y_j - d_j$ up to (i) sign convention (Le Cun maximises $-C$, Rumelhart descends $E$) and (ii) the factor-of-two from Le Cun using $(D-X)^T(D-X)$ vs Rumelhart's $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum(y-d)^2$. Identical mathematical content.

Backward recursion. Le Cun's $B_p(k) = W^T(k+1) \nabla F_k(A_p(k+1)) B_p(k+1)$ and the change-of-variable form $Y_p(k) = \nabla F_k(A_p(k)) W^T(k+1) Y_p(k+1)$ together encode the same recursion that Rumelhart factor into two steps: $\partial E/\partial x_j = \partial E/\partial y_j \cdot y_j(1-y_j)$ (sigmoid-derivative multiplication) and $\partial E/\partial y_i = \sum_j \partial E/\partial x_j \cdot w_{ji}$ (linear backward sum). Composing the Rumelhart pair reproduces Le Cun's recursion when $f$ is the logistic. EP206.7 corresponds to the boundary case at $k=N$.

Stationarity $\nabla L = 0$ and its decomposition into three subconditions $\partial L/\partial B = 0$, $\partial L/\partial X = 0$, $\partial L/\partial W = 0$ are organising principles of Le Cun's derivation. Rumelhart et al. proceed by direct partial-differentiation and never write a stationarity statement; the structural decomposition is implicit in their Eqs. (4)-(7) but not stated as a unified condition.

Gradient-descent weight update. Le Cun's $W(k) \leftarrow W(k) + \lambda \sum_p Y_p(k) X_p^T(k-1)$ combines Rumelhart's per-weight gradient $\partial E/\partial w_{ji} = \partial E/\partial x_j \cdot y_i$ (EP207.6) with the descent step $\Delta w = -\varepsilon \partial E/\partial w$ (EP207.8). Sign flip again from minimise-vs-maximise convention; identical update.
Momentum / acceleration $\Delta w(t) = -\varepsilon \partial E/\partial w(t) + \alpha \Delta w(t-1)$ is a Rumelhart-side practical addition with no Le Cun counterpart in this paper.

The Pineda-Almeida fixed-point gradient ODE is cited prior work that Le Cun re-derives via his Lagrangian formalism. Rumelhart et al.'s only treatment of recurrence is BPTT (ExP207.3), which is computationally distinct from the continuous-time fixed-point method.

Both formalise BP as an optimisation problem. Rumelhart's ProbP207.2 is the unconstrained 'minimise $E(w)$' problem; Le Cun's ProbP206.1 is the explicitly constrained version 'minimise $C(X(N))$ subject to forward dynamics' which the Lagrangian then converts to an unconstrained Lagrange-function problem. Equivalent at the optimum but framed differently.

The 'learn appropriate hidden-unit representations' framing is a Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams contribution that motivates the entire paper. Le Cun's framework does not foreground representation learning; his motivating question is the variational structure of BP.
The Bryson-Ho two-point boundary value problem is a cited optimal-control problem that motivates Le Cun's Lagrangian re-derivation. No counterpart in Rumelhart et al.

Both algorithm nodes describe the back-propagation algorithm for layered networks: a forward pass, a backward pass propagating error derivatives, and a gradient-descent weight update. Inputs (training set, weights, learning rate, sigmoid) and outputs (updated weights minimising squared error) match. Le Cun derives the three passes from stationarity of $L$; Rumelhart et al. derive them by direct chain rule. Same computational procedure.

Composite L1-vs-L2 alignment per v2 rule 2: Le Cun's algorithm is summarised in a single pseudocode block with no step-level decomposition, while Rumelhart et al.'s algorithm is extracted as seven explicit steps (init, forward, output deriv, backward pass, weight grad, update, iterate). Steps 2-6 implement the same forward / backward / update equations matched in EP-level matches above; steps 1 (random init) and 7 (sweep loop) are Rumelhart-side specific implementation details with no separately-extracted Le Cun counterpart.
Bryson-Ho multistage optimal-control procedure is cited external prior work for Le Cun. Rumelhart et al. do not cite or use the optimal-control framing.
Pineda-Almeida recurrent BP is external work re-derived by Le Cun. Rumelhart et al.'s recurrent treatment (ExP207.3) is BPTT, a different algorithm.

The proposition that stationarity $\nabla L = 0$ decomposes into the three passes of BP is the central structural theorem of Le Cun's paper and has no proposition-level counterpart in Rumelhart et al.

Le Cun's structural lemma 'Jacobian $\nabla F_k$ is diagonal with entries $f'(a_{ip})$' is the abstract justification for the per-component sigmoid derivative. Rumelhart et al. simply apply this fact in EP207.5 ($\partial E/\partial x_j = \partial E/\partial y_j \cdot y_j(1-y_j)$, where $y_j(1-y_j)$ is the logistic derivative) without stating it as a separate proposition. Same content, different granularity of presentation.
The Lagrangian/Hamiltonian recovery of Pineda-Almeida recurrent BP is unique to Le Cun.
Le Cun's proof 'derivation of BP from the three subconditions' has no proof counterpart in Rumelhart et al., who present the equations directly without an explicit derivation block.
The variational derivation of recurrent BP is a Le-Cun-specific proof object.

The cited perceptron-convergence procedure (Rosenblatt; Minsky-Papert) used by Rumelhart et al. to motivate hidden-layer learning is not referenced in Le Cun's paper. (External-origin node, but listed because it is a Level-1 theorem; could be omitted but kept here for symmetry with Rumelhart-side perspective.)
